name: Hittite religion
info: Hittite religion was the belief and cult of the Hittites, who created an empire centred in Anatolia from about 1600 to 1180 BCE; it centred on a king who was also priest, a multitude of local gods, and storm-god and sun-goddess myths.

facts.origin: Anatolia, in the Hittite empire centred there from c. 1600 to 1180 BCE, with its capital at Hattusa; a mix of Hattian, Hurrian and Hittite influences
facts.founder: none: a religion of a kingdom, drawing on Hattian, Hurrian and Mesopotamian traditions, with no single founder named
facts.scriptures: no canonical scriptures: the surviving tablets are cult inventories, temple and ritual administration, diviners' reports, rituals and fragments of myth, some used in training scribes
facts.followers: none: the religion ended with the Hittite empire c. 1180 BCE, when the Hittite sites were burned

t: The king was also priest, the figure between gods and people, and after death he was deified; the gods in turn were bound to provide for the people if they were worshipped properly.
The Hittites spoke of a thousand gods, many of them only names today, and many towns kept their own storm-gods instead of identifying them with one national figure.

Much that would give a balanced view is lost: there are no canonical scriptures and no theological discourses, and what is known rests on administrative tablets, carvings, seal stones and temple plans.
dyk: The Hittites sometimes worshipped their gods through Huwasi stones, which represented deities and were treated as sacred objects; gods were often shown standing on the backs of their animals.
ev: The Hittites create an empire centred in Anatolia, which lasts until about 1180 BCE
The queen and priestess Puduhepa works on organising and rationalising her people's religion

sections.origins:
Hittite mythology and religion were the beliefs and practices of the Hittites, who created an empire centred in Anatolia from about 1600 to 1180 BCE. The religion draws on ancient Mesopotamian religion, yet that of the Hittites and Luwians retains noticeable elements of reconstructed Proto-Indo-European mythology. Hittite mythology is described as a mix of Hattian, Hurrian and Hittite influences, and Mesopotamian and Canaanite influences enter Anatolian mythology through Hurrian mythology.

The Hurrians were a neighbouring civilisation close to Anatolia, and their mythology was so closely related that Oxford University Press published a guide to mythology that categorised Hittite and Hurrian mythology together as "Hittite-Hurrian". No details of a Hittite creation myth are known, but scholars speculate that a Hattian mother goddess, believed to be connected to the "great goddess" concept known from the Neolithic site of Çatalhöyük, may have been a consort of the Anatolian storm god.

Hittite tablets on mythology often date from toward the end of the Old Hittite Kingdom, with significantly fewer sources beyond that, and much of what is known comes from artistic rather than textual sources, which makes specific details hard to establish.
sections.beliefs:
The Hittites referred to their own "thousand gods", of whom a great many appear in inscriptions but remain nothing more than names. Gods were often depicted standing on the backs of their beasts, or may have been identifiable in animal form, and the Hittites often worshipped them through Huwasi stones, which represented deities and were treated as sacred objects.

The storm god Tarhunt fought the serpent Illuyanka, a conflict that resembles that of Indra and Vritra in Vedic mythology and of Thor and Jörmungandr in Norse mythology. Tarhunt's consort was the Hattic sun goddess of Arinna, and their children were Telipinu and Inara. The goddess Ishtar, adopted from Mesopotamia, was assimilated through association with similar deities, and in purification rituals her affinity for the underworld was used to cast her as a protector.

The Hittites did not perform regularly scheduled ceremonies to appease the gods, but held rituals in answer to hard times or to mark occasions. Many rituals were based on myth and often involved performing the stories. Many were performed at pits, which represented closeness to chthonic gods; this kind of pit ritual is called "necromantic" because it attempted to commune with gods of the Underworld. Individuals often simply made requests of the gods, without rituals or priests, when the occasion was casual.
sections.texts:
In the words quoted for the religion, "there are no canonical scriptures, no theological disquisitions or discourses, no aids to private devotion". Most surviving texts come from scribes in the royal administration, who kept records on temple organisation, cultic administration and the reports of diviners. Some religious documents formed part of the corpus with which young scribes were trained, and most of those that survive date from the last several decades before the final burning of the sites. Groups of documents called "cult inventories" are valuable for seeing how myth and practice entered daily life.

Many myths involve a large cast of characters, because the central problem has widespread effects, and they resemble action-based epics with an ensemble cast more than morality tales. In the Telipinu myth the disappearance of the god of agriculture and fertility makes all fertility fail, until a bee sent by the goddess Hannahannah finds and stings him, and the goddess Kamrusepa calms him with healing and magic. The Slaying of the Dragon was recited at New Year rituals meant to ensure agricultural prosperity: the goddess Inara and a mortal, Ḫupašiya, trick the serpent, and the Storm God then slays it. The Song of Kumarbi, in which Kumarbi is the father of Tarhunt, is reminiscent of Cronus in Hesiod's Theogony.
sections.spread:
The Hittites had a habit of adopting gods from other pantheons, as other kingdoms of the time did. The Mesopotamian goddess Ishtar, celebrated at her temple at Ain Dara, was one of many adopted deities assimilated into Hittite pantheons, and with her absorption or close association of other goddesses, among them Anzili, Šawuška and Geštinanna, her power and popularity grew. The Hittites made a ritual that treats her as an international goddess, and the differences between outside deities like her were respected even though she had been appropriated for Hittite use.

Influence also went outward. There seem to be traces of Hittite and Anatolian deities that dispersed westward into Aeolis and Doreis, and the Luwian god of weather and lightning, Pihassassa, may be at the origin of the Greek Pegasus. Depictions of hybrid animals such as hippogriffs and chimerae are typical of Anatolian art of the period.

Within the empire, traditions and the status of local cults were constantly changing for lack of a national standard for ritual practice. Beckman (1989) observes that many Hittite towns maintained individual storm-gods, declining to identify them as manifestations of a single national figure; the multiplicity is attributed to a Hittite resistance to syncretisation, and doubtless to the social and political localisation of the empire.
sections.community:
The figure mediating between the worlds of gods and people was the king and priest. A ritual from the Hittite Old Kingdom has the king say that the Sun-God and the Storm-God have entrusted to him the land and his household, so that he should protect them. The king made a point of observing every cult site and temple on his lands, as his duty to the gods and his people, and once he died he was deified. Smaller festivals did not always require the priest-king's presence, so local places had more leeway in worship.

Duties ran both ways: the gods had to provide for the people if they were being worshipped properly, and without dedicated practice from mortals they could not function. King Mursili II made a plea to the gods at a time of struggle in the land. He said that all the land of Hatti was dying, that the ploughmen, miller-women, cowherds and shepherds who served the gods had died, so that offerings were cut off, and he asked why the gods held the people culpable.

The city of Arinna, a day's march from Hattusa, was perhaps the major cult centre and certainly that of the major sun goddess, known as the sun goddess of Arinna. The Hittites also used the will of the gods to justify human actions, in a way similar to the ancient Egyptians.
sections.legacy:
Hittite religion ended with the Hittite empire, and little of it survives in narrative form: most of the narratives of Hittite mythology are lost, and the tablets recovered at the capital Hattusa and other sites lack the elements that would give a balanced view. What is known comes from tablets, stone carvings, seal stones and the ground plans of temples, along with a few images of deities.

Scholars have compared its myths with others. The conflict of Tarhunt and Illuyanka resembles that of Indra and Vritra, that of Thor and Jörmungandr and the daily struggle of Ra and Apophis in Egyptian mythology. Ullikummi, a stone monster fathered by Kumarbi, is otherwise vaguely reminiscent of Hesiod's Typhon, and the Luwian god Pihassassa may be at the origin of Pegasus.

In the 13th century BCE, the queen and priestess Puduhepa worked on organising and rationalising her people's religion. In an inscription she invokes the sun goddess of Arinna, queen of all lands, who in the land of Hatti has that name and in the land of cedars the name Hebat. Such efforts toward syncretism are among the few explicit ones that appear in inscriptions.

summary: Hittite religion was the cult of an Anatolian empire that lasted from about 1600 to 1180 BCE. The king served as priest, the gods were many and often local, and storm-god and sun-goddess myths were told and enacted. Most narratives are lost; what remains is chiefly administrative.
notes: Dates: the article gives only the empire's span, 'c. 1600-1180 BC', and says the sites had a 'final burning'; start -1600 circa and end -1180 circa follow that. It does not date the religion separately from the empire.

Key events: the article gives few dates. Besides the empire's span and the 13th-century Puduhepa material, the 1989 entry is Beckman's scholarly observation, kept for lack of other dated events. Mursili II's plea, the Old Kingdom ritual and the cult inventories are undated in the article.

Left out: the list of Hittite deities (empty in the saved text), the Nerik storm god's detail beyond the faith map, the wording 'Hittite-Hurrian' beyond a mention. The article says 'Hurrian religion' and 'Luwian religion' in See also only.
The Telipinu myth: the article gives two endings (Kamrusepa calms him, or a mortal priest prays for his anger to be sent to bronze containers in the underworld); only the first is told in texts.
The article contradicts itself a little on the king's priestly role over local worship (the king observes every cult site; smaller festivals did not need him); both stated.

Faith map: the article gives no dates for Nerik, Ain Dara or Arinna, so the Nerik mark sits at about 1250 BCE (the 13th-century Puduhepa material) as an approximation, and Ain Dara and Arinna are not marked, Arinna having no coordinates the article gives. No routes: the article gives no dated route.
